title: Pushing the Limit of Quantum Mechanical Simulation to the Raman Spectra of a Biological System with 100 Million Atoms
problem: Quantum mechanical simulations of Raman spectra require expensive computation of molecular response properties at scale, making accurate simulations of large biological systems computationally prohibitive. Previous approaches could only handle systems of a few million atoms.
motivation: Enabling quantum mechanical Raman spectroscopy simulation for large biological systems provides detailed structural and chemical characterization impossible with current methods, supporting materials discovery and biological analysis.
method: The authors developed efficient quantum mechanical algorithms and optimized implementations on heterogeneous supercomputing architectures (Sunway and ORISE). They achieved near-linear strong and weak scaling through careful algorithmic design, massive parallelization across thousands of nodes, and optimized communication and memory management patterns.
key_novelty: First ab initio quantum mechanical Raman spectra simulation demonstrating near-linear scalability to 100 million atom biological systems across tens of thousands of compute nodes.
contributions: Efficient quantum mechanical algorithms enabling large-scale Raman spectra computation
Nearly linear scaling achieved on 96K-node Sunway (400 PFLOPS) and 6K-node ORISE (85 PFLOPS) supercomputers
Demonstrated capability to simulate 100 million atom biological systems
Optimized implementations bridging quantum chemistry methods to extreme-scale HPC systems

metrics.speedup: nearly linear strong and weak scaling
metrics.other: 400 PFLOPS peak FP64 (Sunway, 96K nodes), 85 PFLOPS peak FP64 (ORISE, 6K nodes)

limitations: Scalability limits beyond 100 million atoms and hardware portability constraints are not discussed.
